Saed Ismail Amiri pleaded guilty to wire fraud over a scheme to defraud the Afghan government of more than $100 million on a power substation contract.

key_claims: By 21 July 2021 the Taliban controlled about half of Afghanistan's 419 districts, more than double the number a month earlier.
The Taliban seized border crossings at Sher Khan (Tajikistan), Islam Qala (Iran) and Spin Boldak (Pakistan), controlling at least six crossings by press time.
The ANDSF appeared surprised and unready and was on its back foot, though the government still held all 34 provincial capitals.
U.S. and coalition forces withdrew nearly all troops, with fewer than a thousand U.S. personnel remaining, versus 110,000 a decade earlier.
Civilian casualties hit a record high in May and June 2021 according to UNAMA.
SIGAR assessed the overall trend as clearly unfavorable to the Afghan government, which could face an existential crisis.
CSTC-A implemented only one of six SIGAR recommendations from 2018 on ANDSF fuel accountability.
DOD spent $3.74 billion on ANDSF fuel from FY2010 to FY2020 and plans a further $1.45 billion through FY2025.
CSTC-A's plan to transition fuel responsibility to the Afghan government lacked adequate analysis and controls.
USAID's Goldozi Project missed its training, employment and income targets, and COVID-19 further curtailed it.
SIGAR financial audits questioned $494 million in costs, and agencies allowed $389 million of the $417 million on which they made determinations.
SIGAR's seven financial audits this quarter found $739,105 in questioned costs.
SIGAR found that agencies emphasized tracking program outputs over assessing outcomes and impacts in reconstruction contracting monitoring and evaluation.
SIGAR has 94 ongoing investigations and 160 criminal convictions to date.
SIGAR has closed about 91% of its 1,176 recommendations issued from 2009 through June 2021.
The Taliban launched an offensive overrunning district centers but avoided attacking U.S. and Coalition forces during the withdrawal.
The Taliban seized key border crossings, potentially denying the Afghan government significant customs revenue.
Afghan government–Taliban peace talks remained stalled and Eid al-Fitr ceasefires had no enduring effect.
USFOR-A responsibility passed to CENTCOM commander McKenzie on July 12, 2021 as Resolute Support drew down.
SIGAR recommends reestablishing an Afghanistan Threat Finance Cell targeting narcotics and terrorist financial networks.
As of 30 Jun 2021 the US had appropriated about $144.98 billion for Afghan reconstruction, $88.61 billion of it for security.
ASFF accounted for $82.90 billion appropriated, with $75.20 billion disbursed.
DOD reports $837.3 billion cumulative war obligations; the Costs of War Project estimates $2.26 trillion.
About $17.28 billion in US on-budget assistance has gone to the Afghan government and multilateral trust funds since 2002.
CSTC-A transitioned its ANDSF-building role to the Qatar-based DSCMO-A in the quarter.
ASFF FY2020 and FY2021 budgets are about $3.1 billion and $3.05 billion, with the FY2022 request at $3.33 billion.
The NATO ANA Trust Fund has contributed nearly $1.70 billion to ASFF, of which about $1.16 billion had been disbursed by June 30, 2021.
CERP is being phased out: the FY2021 appropriation fell to $2 million, with cumulative funding of about $3.71 billion.
DICDA counterdrug funding for Afghanistan dropped to zero in FY2021, with cumulative funding of $3.28 billion.
ESF allocations for Afghanistan have declined (from $350M in FY2019 to $136.45M in FY2021), while disbursements exceed allocations.
INCLE, MRA and NADR cumulative funding stand at more than $5.50 billion, $1.60 billion and $927 million respectively.
NADR allocation for Afghanistan for FY 2021 was $45.80 million, up 19% from FY 2020.
Cumulative contributions to the seven multilateral organizations since 2002 total $37.96 billion, of which the US gave $9.87 billion.
ARTF is the largest channel of international support for the Afghan government's budgets, with $13.07 billion paid in by 34 donors.
US contributions to LOTFA have been significantly reduced since 2018.
NATO said RSM would enter a 'new chapter' of financial support, out-of-country training, a diplomatic presence in Kabul and funding for Hamid Karzai International Airport.
The Taliban launched an offensive from May 2021, overrunning dozens of district centers and border crossings while avoiding attacks on U.S. and Coalition forces.
Northern provinces, once anti-Taliban bastions, fell rapidly to the Taliban.
CSTC-A ended on 12 July 2021 and was replaced by DSCMO-A in Qatar providing over-the-horizon support.
About 1,600 ANDSF personnel fled to Tajikistan from Badakhshan in July 2021.
Local elders sometimes mediated truces letting ANDSF leave, with U.S.-supplied equipment seized by the Taliban for propaganda.
Ghani replaced his defense and interior ministers on 19 June 2021 amid the deteriorating security situation.
The Taliban offensive accelerated in June-July 2021, capturing dozens of district centers and at least six international border crossings.
LWJ estimated the Taliban controlled 221 districts by July 15, 2021, up from 73 on April 14.
Gen. Milley said on July 21 that strategic momentum appeared to be with the Taliban.
Taliban control of border crossings deprives the government of customs revenue and gives the Taliban more revenue opportunities.
RS attributed about 93% of April-May 2021 civilian casualties to antigovernment forces: 40% Taliban, 38% unknown insurgents, 14% IS-K, under 1% Haqqani Network.
US officials believe IS-K carried out the 8 May 2021 attack on a Shia girls' school in Kabul, which the Taliban disavowed.
Enemy-initiated attacks rose significantly after the February 2020 US-Taliban agreement.
About 650 US troops will remain to protect US Embassy Kabul, down from 2,500 the previous quarter.
CENTCOM estimated over 90% of the US retrograde complete by July 5, 2021, with Bagram handed to the Afghan MOD.
Security assistance is now delivered over-the-horizon from Qatar by DSCMO-A, constraining US monitoring of ANDSF use of ASFF funds.
DOD could not provide much reconstruction data, including ANDSF operational performance, because train, advise, assist missions ended in early May.
ANDSF strength reported (300,699) does not reflect losses from the Taliban offensive from May to July 2021.
ANA killed-in-action reports trended upward, especially in June 2021; at least 26 insider attacks on ANDSF occurred April-June 2021.
Local power brokers in the north mobilizing militias raised fears of a 1990s-style civil war.
Taliban offensive and the withdrawal of US contractors reduced AAF aircraft readiness in June 2021.
The Taliban was reported to be assassinating Afghan pilots off-base.
US forces handed over major bases, including Bagram Airfield, to the Afghan MOD between May and July 2021.
ANDSF suffered at least 26 insider attacks in Q2 2021 with at least 81 killed.
Only 15 of 42 AAF aircrew positions were filled with qualified personnel.
Taliban offensive and US/Coalition withdrawal sharply reduced Afghan Air Force readiness in June 2021.
The Taliban is reportedly assassinating Afghan pilots off-base.

The Taliban have not engaged with the Afghan government's ceasefire, power-sharing and elections plan for nearly 10 months, per Atmar.
The UN reported the Taliban captured 50 of 370 districts since the start of May 2021.
The Taliban may believe they can achieve military victory given recent battlefield success and the US withdrawal.
Afghan government reported the Taliban destroyed 260 government administrative buildings in 106 Taliban-held districts.
World Bank evaluators concluded ARTF service delivery failed to foster Afghan state legitimacy even as conflict intensity remained at record levels.
The Taliban escalated demands on World Bank-funded health services, causing 20% of Sehatmandi facilities to close.
Armed opposition groups controlled community council sites in nine provinces, including districts containing provincial capitals; 59% of planned councils were not established.
IARCSC reported the Taliban seized government buildings in 29 provinces and left 50,000 civil servants unable to work.
About 70% of US on-budget assistance goes to Afghan security forces requirements.

Drug seizures and arrests have had minimal impact on opium cultivation and production.
Counternarcotics High Commission has not met since its inaugural meeting in February 2020.
As of May 31, 2021, 5,330 national-security threat inmates were held in OPA-run prisons.
USAID rejected multiple AMANAT grant proposals for failing to show how interventions would reduce corruption.
INL and DEA plan to sustain support for Afghan counternarcotics units after the U.S. military withdrawal.
INL has disbursed $44.2 million to DEA to support the NIU and SIU as of February 2021.
UNODC could verify only very small amounts of eradication, in Nangarhar.
Conflict-induced displacement in Afghanistan was 101% higher than a year earlier by July 2021.
Rural women interviewed by AAN held varied views of Taliban control and peace.
Taliban operate illegal vehicle checkpoints searching for individuals associated with international organizations and the government, impeding USAID project implementation.
SIGAR assesses that future U.S. reconstruction will be hindered by insecurity and political instability rather than by unwillingness to fund it.
No agreement had been reached to keep Hamid Karzai International Airport in Kabul open after the troop withdrawal; HKIA transfer date was still under review.
The U.S. provided approximately $36.3 billion for governance and economic and social development in Afghanistan since 2002.
The Taliban rejected any continued Turkish military presence at HKIA, calling it a violation of the February 2020 US-Taliban agreement.
The ACAA lacks the capacity to run Afghan airports without NATO and donor support.

Illegal mining has become a key revenue source for the Taliban, which issue licenses, tax operations and control smuggling to Pakistan.
The Taliban seized six border crossings in the quarter, including four major ones, threatening Afghan government customs revenue.
Border crossings in Herat, Kandahar and Kunduz generated 34.3% of Afghan customs revenue in FY 1399.
More than half of goods crossing the border flow to the informal economy, benefiting insurgents and corrupt officials.
Afghanistan relies on donor grants for most public expenditure and has a large trade deficit.
Border crossings in Herat, Kandahar and Kunduz generated 34.3% of Afghan government customs revenue in FY 1399.
More than half the value of goods crossing the border flows to the informal economy, a major income source for insurgents and corrupt officials.
The Taliban kept the Sher Khan Bandar crossing open to trade and began collecting customs revenue there.
USAID suspended subcontractor Relief International over strong indications of breaching antiterrorism and terrorist-financing rules.
USAID suspended and RADP-East terminated subcontractor Relief International over suspected antiterrorism and terrorist-financing breaches.
Militants increasingly targeted electricity pylons, disrupting supply in Kabul and seven other provinces, though USAID said no U.S.-funded power infrastructure was affected.
DABS could not collect electricity payments in Taliban-controlled areas of several provinces, where the Taliban collected the fees.
Reports indicate the Taliban threatened that girls should not attend school beyond the seventh grade in areas under their control.
Afghanistan relies heavily on electricity imports from Iran, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, making supply vulnerable.
The Afghan government blamed the Taliban for the 8 May 2021 Kabul school bombing, but the Taliban denied involvement and no group claimed it.
